analysis.one_liner: Sends hourly workers a refundable federal check covering half the gap between their wage and $16.50 an hour.
analysis.headline: The wage-supplement tax credit never got a hearing or vote in the Senate Finance Committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a refundable tax credit — the 'Blue Collar Bonus' — equal to half the gap between a worker's hourly wage and the median wage (set at $16.50 an hour, adjusted for inflation). Workers earning below that rate would get the bonus for every hour worked, up to 2,080 hours a year, with payments available quarterly rather than only at tax time. It was introduced by Sen. Josh Hawley in March 2021 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it sat until the Congress expired.
analysis.who_benefits: Hourly and salaried workers earning below the median wage — about $16.50 an hour or less — gain a direct federal supplement of 50 cents for every dollar their wage falls short of that benchmark, up to 40 hours a week. A full-time worker earning $13 an hour, for example, would receive roughly $3,640 a year. Because the credit is refundable and paid in advance, it reaches workers even if they owe little or no federal income tax.

how_it_helps.text: Refundable credit covers half the gap between a worker's average hourly wage and the $16.50 median wage, with an annual cap of 2,080 hours worked [S3][S2].
Advance payments quarterly, not only at tax filing, so the boost reaches households during the year [S2][S3].
Wage floor is inflation-adjusted, preventing erosion of the benefit over time [S3].

Includes protections to reduce overpayment risk: a safe-harbor limit on recapturing overpaid advances for lower-income filers, and a 2-year disqualification for prior fraudulent or reckless claims [S3].

analysis.who_pays: All federal taxpayers bear the cost. The bill does not include a revenue offset, so the credit's cost would add to the federal deficit or require spending cuts elsewhere. The bill also imposes compliance work on employers, who must report additional wage and hours data to the IRS so advance payments can be calculated.

drawbacks.text: No revenue offset: the bill adds a permanent-cost tax credit (through 2023 in this version) without funding it, increasing federal deficits unless paired with other legislation [S3].
Requires extensive employer wage-and-hours reporting to the IRS for advance payments, a new compliance burden particularly on small businesses and multiple-employer workers [S3].
Requires Social Security numbers issued to U.S. citizens or qualifying categories to claim the credit, excluding many nonresident and some immigrant workers [S3].

The credit could interact with wage-setting: the bill directs the Treasury Secretary and Labor Department to write rules to prevent employers from cutting wages or hours because the credit effectively subsidizes low pay [S3].
Workers with volatile wages or irregular hours could face significant overpayment clawbacks at tax time, a risk that plagued advance payments under the expanded Child Tax Credit [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The credit is a real, direct income boost for low-wage workers, and its design is more careful than many tax credits — refundable, inflation-adjusted, paid in advance, with explicit anti-fraud and employer-substitution rules. But it is unpayed-for, and the administrative lift (employer wage-data reporting, quarterly recalculations) is substantial. Whether it is a good deal depends on whether one accepts deficit financing for a targeted wage supplement, and on whether the anti-abuse rules hold up in practice.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in March 2021; the committee never acted on it, and it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Josh Hawley introduced the Blue Collar Bonus Act on March 2, 2021 [S1][S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day, with no further action recorded afterward [S5].
The 117th Congress ended January 3, 2023, without the bill receiving a committee hearing, markup, floor vote, or any consideration in the House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained materially from the bill's failure. Low-wage workers lost a potential income supplement; the bill simply lapsed without opposition ever having to take a public position on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the bill simply lapsed

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and had it referred to the Senate Finance Committee.

sides.party_line_note: No floor vote, committee vote, or cosponsor ever positioned the parties on the bill, so no partisan split can be measured.
